4.modern-en: Pericles appears leading Athenian forces in the revolt of Euboea and the war against Samos, commanding the fleet that defeats Samian ships off Tragia — an early demonstration of his generalship in the years before the main war.

5.modern-en: Pericles is the dominant figure in Athenian deliberations as Sparta's ultimatums arrive. He carries a motion barring Spartan envoys from addressing the assembly and delivers a major speech urging Athens to hold firm, reject Spartan demands, and enter the war with confidence.

6.modern-en: Pericles shapes Athens's war strategy from the outset: he bars his personal friend Archidamus from sparing his estate (to prevent any suspicion of favoritism), withholds the Athenians from open battle as Spartan forces ravage Attica, and delivers the celebrated Funeral Oration honoring the war's first dead.

7.modern-en: As Athenians suffer the plague and blame Pericles for the war, he faces a hostile assembly. He delivers a defiant speech defending his strategy, is fined by the courts, but is re-elected general — and dies of the plague shortly after, leaving Athens without its guiding hand.

3.modern-en: At the congress of the Peloponnesian League debating whether to declare war, Archidamus delivers a measured speech urging caution. He warns that Athens is wealthy, experienced at sea, and not easily defeated quickly — and argues that war should not be rushed into without better preparation.

6.modern-en: Archidamus leads the first Peloponnesian invasion of Attica, commanding the assembled forces across the Isthmus. He lingers near the border hoping to provoke the Athenians into battle, then methodically ravages the Attic plain when they refuse to come out.

7.modern-en: Archidamus leads the second invasion of Attica, pressing deeper into the countryside. His army ravages both coastal and inland districts as the plague tears through the city, though the Athenians still refuse a pitched battle on land.

8.modern-en: Archidamus turns his forces against Plataea, a small Athenian ally. He receives Plataean envoys, delivers an ultimatum demanding they break with Athens, and when refused begins a prolonged siege, constructing a great mound against the walls.

9.modern-en: Archidamus leads the fourth invasion of Attica, ravaging the country as usual while the Athenians pursue their naval strategy and avoid land battle — the war's early strategic pattern holding firm.

epithet.en: Athenian hero of Salamis, later exile
epithet.da: Athensk helt fra Salamis, siden landflygtig

1.modern-en: Thucydides briefly credits Themistocles as the architect of Athenian sea power, noting that the Corinthians were the first to build triremes in Greece and that Athens's naval dominance — which Themistocles championed — laid the foundation for everything that followed.

3.modern-en: An Athenian speaker at the Peloponnesian congress reminds the allies of Themistocles's decisive role at Salamis, where Athens contributed the largest fleet and its ablest commander, saving all of Hellas from the Persians.

4.modern-en: Themistocles engineers the rapid fortification of Athens after the Persian Wars, tricking Spartan envoys while the walls are raised. He is later ostracized, moves to Argos, is accused of treason through his association with the disgraced Spartan regent Pausanias, and flees.

5.modern-en: Thucydides recounts Themistocles's flight in full: hunted by Athens and Sparta alike, he crosses to Persia, writes to King Artaxerxes presenting himself as a benefactor, and receives an honored place at the Persian court — dying there, some say by his own hand to avoid fulfilling his promises against Greece.

epithet.en: Spartan regent and hero of Plataea
epithet.da: Spartansk regent og helt fra Platæa

4.modern-en: Pausanias commands the Greek forces at Byzantium after the Persian Wars, initially victorious but soon recalled to Sparta amid complaints from the allies about his arrogance. His overbearing conduct drives the allies to transfer leadership to Athens.

5.modern-en: Thucydides details Pausanias's treasonous correspondence with the Persian king, his adoption of Persian dress and manners, and his eventual undoing: cornered by Spartan ephors who trick him into a self-incriminating conversation, he takes refuge in a temple and is walled in until he starves to death.

epithet.en: Athenian admiral of the Corinthian Gulf
epithet.da: Athensk admiral i Den Korinthiske Golf

8.modern-en: Phormio commands the Athenian naval squadron at Naupactus and wins two remarkable victories over a much larger Peloponnesian fleet in the Corinthian Gulf. By keeping his ships moving in tight circles to create confusion and waiting for the morning sea-breeze to disorder the enemy, he routs first forty-seven, then seventy-seven ships with just twenty — among the war's most celebrated naval feats.

9.modern-en: Cleon dominates the Athenian assembly debate over Mytilene. He argues fiercely for executing the entire adult male population of the rebel city as an example to other allies, calling mercy a dangerous weakness. His motion passes initially, then is reversed the next day in a second vote after Diodotus makes a pragmatic counter-argument.

12.modern-en: Cleon pushes Athens to press the siege of Sphacteria rather than accept Spartan peace overtures. When Nicias calls his bluff by offering him a command, he takes it, and achieves the stunning capture of the Spartan hoplites on the island — a feat that silences his critics and inflates his reputation for generalship.

14.modern-en: Cleon is mentioned as the reason Brasidas proceeds carefully with the armistice provisions — the Athenian demagogue is determined to prevent peace while Athens holds Spartan prisoners, sensing the diplomatic leverage it provides.

15.modern-en: Cleon sails to Thrace to recover the cities lost to Brasidas. After initial successes, he is caught off guard by a sudden Spartan sortie from Amphipolis and killed in the rout — his death, alongside Brasidas's, removes the chief hawks on both sides and opens the door to the Peace of Nicias.

9.modern-en: Diodotus delivers the great counter-argument in the Mytilenian Debate, opposing Cleon's demand for mass execution. He argues on purely pragmatic grounds — not mercy — that killing all Mytilenians would remove Athens's best asset: the ordinary people of allied cities who will always side with Athens against their own oligarchs if given the chance. His motion narrowly wins, and a second ship races to cancel the order.

epithet.en: Spartan general and liberator of Thrace

10.modern-en: Brasidas appears as adviser to the Peloponnesian fleet sent to assist the Corcyraean oligarchs. He urges bold action but the fleet commander hesitates, and the opportunity passes — Brasidas's energy already contrasting with more cautious Spartan colleagues.

12.modern-en: Brasidas is named by Thucydides as one of three Spartan commissioners sent to stiffen the fleet after Phormio's victories, tasked with raising morale and preparing for a rematch at sea.

14.modern-en: Brasidas leads a remarkable overland march through Thessaly to reach Thrace, then wins over city after city — Acanthus, Amphipolis, Torone — through a combination of military skill and persuasive speeches promising freedom from Athenian rule. His capture of Amphipolis in a night march is the campaign's masterstroke and causes panic in Athens.

15.modern-en: Brasidas faces Cleon's counter-expedition to Thrace. He maneuvers patiently before Amphipolis, then launches a sudden surprise sortie that routs the Athenians — and falls wounded in the pursuit. He is carried into the city alive, learns of the victory, and dies. Amphipolis honors him as a founder and hero.

epithet.en: Athenian general, architect of the Peace — and Sicily's ruin
epithet.da: Athensk general, fredens arkitekt — og Siciliens ødelægger

12.modern-en: Nicias is the senior general at Pylos. When he mockingly offers Cleon his command, and Cleon accepts, Nicias steps aside — inadvertently handing the demagogue the glory of capturing the Spartan soldiers on Sphacteria.

15.modern-en: With Cleon and Brasidas both dead, Nicias emerges as the leading Athenian advocate for peace. He negotiates and signs the treaty that bears his name — the Peace of Nicias — ending the first phase of the war, though its terms prove contested from the start.

18.modern-en: Nicias opposes the Sicilian Expedition in the assembly as reckless overreach, but his strategy of demanding vast forces to deter the vote backfires: the Athenians simply vote him the huge fleet he described, and he is appointed one of three commanders. He sails against his own judgment.

20.modern-en: Nicias is the cautious, methodical commander of the Sicilian force, proceeding slowly to invest Syracuse while his more aggressive colleague Lamachus is killed. He writes a frank dispatch to Athens describing the army's worsening situation and requesting reinforcements or recall.

22.modern-en: After Demosthenes's night assault on Epipolae fails disastrously, Nicias refuses to authorize retreat. Despite the army's misery and disease, he insists on staying — partly from fear of Athenian punishment, partly from secret contacts inside Syracuse who tell him the city is near financial collapse.

23.modern-en: Nicias presides over the final catastrophe. He addresses the demoralized troops before the last sea battle, then leads the doomed retreat by land after the fleet is destroyed. Separated from Demosthenes's division, he finally surrenders to Gylippus at the Assinarus river — and is executed by the Syracusans, against Gylippus's wishes.

epithet.en: Athenian general, bold and often unlucky
epithet.da: Athensk general, dristig og ofte uheldig

11.modern-en: Demosthenes leads an Athenian squadron around the Peloponnese and, persuaded by Messenian allies, attempts to conquer Aetolia as a base for striking Boeotia. The campaign ends in disaster when his light-armed forces are ambushed in dense woodland and cut to pieces — but he redeems himself later the same season by destroying an Ambraciot force at Idomene in a brilliant night attack.

12.modern-en: Demosthenes fortifies Pylos on a sudden initiative and successfully defends it against Spartan naval and land assault. He then plans and leads the surprise landing on Sphacteria with Cleon, maneuvering Spartan forces into a hopeless position and accepting their surrender — one of the war's great tactical coups.

22.modern-en: Demosthenes arrives at Syracuse with substantial reinforcements and immediately pushes for decisive action. His night assault on the Epipolae heights initially goes well but collapses into confused fighting in the dark — his men rout their own allies — ending in failure. He correctly argues for immediate retreat before the army deteriorates further.

23.modern-en: Demosthenes commands the rearguard in the land retreat from Syracuse. His division, moving more slowly, is surrounded and forced to surrender — the survivors imprisoned in the stone quarries. He and Nicias are executed by the Syracusans against Gylippus's wishes.

16.modern-en: Alcibiades emerges as the key Athenian advocate for breaking the Peace of Nicias. He secretly manipulates Spartan envoys before the assembly to discredit them, then brokers an anti-Spartan alliance with Argos, Mantinea, and Elis — and personally campaigns through the Peloponnese to cement it.

17.modern-en: Alcibiades sails to Argos to arrest Spartan sympathizers, reinforcing Athens's grip on its alliance network. Thucydides describes him at the height of his influence — bold, ambitious, and impossible for Athens to resist.

18.modern-en: Alcibiades is the most passionate advocate for the Sicilian Expedition, opposing Nicias in the assembly. He is appointed co-commander but is then charged with mutilating the Hermae and profaning the Mysteries. He sails with the fleet, then is recalled to stand trial — and defects to Sparta instead.

19.modern-en: Recalled from Sicily to face trial, Alcibiades refuses to surrender and flees — first by ship, then to the Peloponnese. Athens convicts him in absentia and condemns him to death. He arrives at Sparta and begins advising the Spartans on how to defeat his own city.

20.modern-en: Alcibiades addresses the Spartan assembly, urging them to fortify Decelea in Attica permanently and to send a capable commander to Syracuse. His inside knowledge of Athenian strategy and psychology makes him their most valuable adviser — if the least trustworthy one.

25.modern-en: In exile among the Persians, Alcibiades plays all sides: he advises Tissaphernes to prolong the war by keeping both Athens and Sparta exhausted, then secretly offers the Athenian fleet at Samos a path back to power if they replace democracy with oligarchy and secure Persian support — engineering his own recall.

26.modern-en: The army at Samos votes to recall Alcibiades and elects him general. He returns from Tissaphernes, claims credit for preventing the Phoenician fleet from reaching the Peloponnesians, and begins levying money and forces — his restoration nearly complete as Thucydides's narrative breaks off.

epithet.en: Syracusan statesman and defender of Sicily

13.modern-en: Hermocrates speaks at the Congress of Gela, persuading the Sicilian cities to make peace among themselves and expel the Athenian forces. His argument — that Sicilians should settle their own affairs without inviting outside powers — succeeds, and Athens's commanders are sent home with nothing gained.

19.modern-en: When news of the Athenian expedition reaches Syracuse, Hermocrates alone takes it seriously. He addresses a skeptical assembly, urging immediate preparation: fortify the city, seek allies, and send envoys to Carthage and Corinth. His warning is largely ignored, but his foresight sets him apart as Syracuse's most perceptive leader.

23.modern-en: After the final sea battle, Hermocrates fears the Athenians will escape by land and regroup elsewhere in Sicily. He persuades the authorities to set ambushes on the roads and sends false messengers to delay the Athenian retreat — the ruse that allows the Syracusans to cut off and destroy the retreating army.

21.modern-en: Gylippus arrives at Syracuse against all odds — having reached the city just before the Athenians close the final gap in their siege wall — and immediately transforms the defense. He builds a counter-wall across Epipolae that defeats the Athenian circumvallation, wins battles by land, leads raids on the harbor forts, and goes into Sicily and southern Italy recruiting fresh troops and ships.

22.modern-en: Gylippus coordinates the Syracusan naval and land operations against the reinforced Athenian army under Demosthenes, pressing them on multiple fronts. As the Athenians debate retreat, his forces keep tightening the siege.

23.modern-en: Gylippus commands the final phase of the campaign: closing the harbor mouth, destroying the Athenian fleet in the Great Harbour, and pursuing the retreating army by land. He accepts Nicias's personal surrender and wants to bring both Athenian generals back to Sparta alive — but the Syracusans execute them over his objection.

epithet.en: Persian satrap of Lydia and Caria
epithet.da: Persisk satrap over Lydien og Karien

24.modern-en: Tissaphernes negotiates treaties with Sparta to fund the Peloponnesian fleet in exchange for Persian sovereignty over territories previously subject to the King. He begins paying the allied sailors but at reduced rates, deliberately keeping both sides exhausted rather than handing decisive victory to either.

25.modern-en: Tissaphernes is manipulated by Alcibiades, who advises him to give neither side enough support to win decisively. When Athenian envoys arrive hoping for a Persian alliance, Alcibiades (speaking through Tissaphernes) makes impossible demands — and the negotiations collapse, leaving Tissaphernes free to play both sides.

26.modern-en: Tissaphernes departs for Aspendus under pretense of bringing the Phoenician fleet to the Peloponnesians, but the fleet never comes. Both sides grow furious at his double-dealing; his payments to Sparta dry up, and he is left discredited by all parties as the war enters its final phase.

24.modern-en: Phrynichus commands the Athenian fleet in operations off Ionia. When colleagues want to fight the arriving Peloponnesian fleet against long odds, he refuses — reasoning that a naval defeat would cost Athens everything, while retreating costs nothing. His tactical caution is sound but earns him enemies.

25.modern-en: Phrynichus secretly betrays his own side to prevent Alcibiades's recall: fearing Alcibiades would take revenge on him, he writes to the Spartan admiral revealing Athenian plans. When exposed, he doubles down — building fortifications at Samos while becoming a key architect of the oligarchic coup in Athens, working with Antiphon and Pisander to install the Four Hundred.

26.modern-en: Phrynichus is assassinated in the agora, stabbed by an unknown assailant — a blow against the oligarchic regime. His death accelerates the Four Hundred's collapse and is later cited as justified given his treasonous dealings with Sparta.

epithet.en: Athenian orator and mastermind of the Four Hundred
epithet.da: Athensk taler og hjerne bag De Fire Hundrede

25.modern-en: Thucydides singles out Antiphon as the true architect of the oligarchic revolution. Unlike Pisander who fronts the movement, Antiphon designs the whole scheme from the shadows — a man of exceptional intelligence who distrusted public life but whose counsel was sought by all, and who later made what Thucydides calls the greatest defense speech ever heard when tried for treason.

26.modern-en: Antiphon is among the Four Hundred's hardliners who negotiate with Sparta behind the regime's back. When the coup collapses after the army at Samos refuses to submit, Antiphon is arrested, tried, and executed — the price of engineering Athens's most radical constitutional rupture.

epithet.en: Athenian politician, critic of the Four Hundred
epithet.da: Athensk politiker, kritiker af De Fire Hundrede

25.modern-en: Theramenes is listed among the leaders of the oligarchic coup that installs the Four Hundred at Athens — though Thucydides hints at his ambivalence even at this stage, as he is associated with those who want a broader constitutional settlement rather than absolute rule by a narrow clique.

26.modern-en: Theramenes breaks openly with the Four Hundred's hardliners, protesting their secret construction of a fort at Eetioneia (suspected of being intended to admit a Spartan fleet) and helping bring down the regime. His opposition precipitates the assembly that votes to replace the Four Hundred with the broader Five Thousand.
